+# Presentation Automation Planning Brief
+
+We have a basic presentation that is not yet rich in content. Each submodule or repository can already provide its own presentation, and those presentations can be combined into one presentation spanning multiple repositories. This is a valuable foundation for the goal of a modular, extensible system.
+
+The next step is to make the presentations informative, understandable, and visually effective. Their primary purpose is to communicate information clearly to readers or listeners, not merely to look attractive.
+
+## Audience and Purpose
+
+The initial audience is software developers who want to write code with AI. The presentation must show how to use the existing repositories for that purpose. It should address human developers and AI agents in the same way: both should be able to understand how the repository is used and how it is intended to be used.
+
+The presentation should provide solution-oriented motivation:
+
+- explain the available tools, their benefits, their design rationale, and recommended uses;
+- present the system as workflow tooling, where each tool has a distinct role within a larger workflow;
+- show how these workflows can improve over time and automate most individual tasks;
+- emphasize that work should run locally where possible, minimizing expensive API usage; and
+- ensure that people can always read the data, follow decisions, and assess quality.
+
+## Presentation Structure
+
+Structure the presentation from the outside inward, introducing topics gradually and increasing detail while preserving consistent long-range context across all slides.
+
+Begin with the learner and the contexts of software development, AI assistants, and a software project. Then explain how the tools relate to one another, followed by the components of each tool. In the long term, the hierarchy may reach individual functions or even lines of code. Understanding context is more important than presenting isolated content.
+
+The presentation and any nested presentations for individual components should use the same global scheme. Each slide must have a clear central statement or task, and every slide should contribute to the overall task: introduce newcomers to the tools, provide the repository vocabulary, and explain how the system can be used.
+
+Include an overview diagram of the information flow and tool sequence in a typical session: from input to an output that fulfils the input requirements. It should show verification loops, planning methods, improvement loops, and how the finished output is produced. This gives newcomers a project-level view before they need to understand every component in detail.
+
+## Automated Repository-Derived Content
+
+Keep natural-language content in the presentation to a minimum. Generate descriptions and representations from repository files and stored entries wherever possible, so the presentation stays current without manual work. Allow presentation-specific choices, such as colours and alternative data representations, to be controlled through a configuration file or a dedicated presentation area.
+
+Investigate automated sources and representations including:
+
+- **Repository and code hierarchy:** Use the still-incomplete `Peek` tool to represent Git repositories, Cargo workspaces, Rust crates, and modules as a hierarchy or graph suitable for presentation. Extend the abstraction represented by an abstract syntax tree so it can include crate hierarchies, Cargo workspaces, and Git repositories.
+- **Selectable detail:** Allow `Peek` to render hierarchy nodes at different resolutions. For example, render a Rust file as a skeleton of defined functions and types; render a crate as its modules; render modules with signatures; or render a Git repository as a tree of packages or crates.
+- **Language scope:** Rust is the primary focus, but the hierarchy should eventually be able to include TypeScript, JavaScript, and Python. The immediate priority is to collect Git repository and crate hierarchies through `Peek` and thereby complete more of its intended functionality.
+- **Documentation:** Consider automatically generated Rust documentation as a source. It might be integrated with `Peek`, although it may not provide sufficient control.
+- **Public tool surfaces:** For MCP and CLI servers, collect and present public or offered commands as lists, trees, diagrams, help output, or individual command slides.
+- **Usage examples:** Present selected tests to demonstrate how tools are used and which behaviour is expected.
+- **Specifications:** Present specification entries, potentially after extending the specification tool to generate presentation-ready representations. In a later direction, specifications could become the bridge from which presentations are generated: a specification defines the repository goal, an implementation fulfils it, documentation describes the implementation, and the specification summarizes the feature for presentation to users.
+
+## Visual Language
+
+Define a global visual vocabulary and a consistent mapping from vocabulary objects to their appearance. Keep that mapping coherent across the whole presentation and across nested component presentations.
+
+Use, where appropriate:
+
+- colour coding;
+- distinct edge styles;
+- a uniform syntax for formal statements;
+- typography-based information coding;
+- diagrams for multi-faceted relationships; and
+- tables and nested lists for many discrete points.
+
+The project has substantial creative freedom to make the presentation clear and compelling, while deriving its content from actual code and memory entries instead of hard-coding it.
+
+## Requested Next Work
+
+Collect the existing information and plans for presentations. Investigate the newly defined ideas, refine them into clearer specifications, plan the implementation and verification steps, and identify open questions or missing specifications. Prioritize capabilities that can be implemented and tested quickly, while planning and preparing lower-priority capabilities for later work.

+# Presentation Automation Planning Brief
+
+We have a basic presentation that is not yet rich in content. Each submodule or repository can already provide its own presentation, and those presentations can be combined into one presentation spanning multiple repositories. This is a valuable foundation for the goal of a modular, extensible system.
+
+The next step is to make the presentations informative, understandable, and visually effective. Their primary purpose is to communicate information clearly to readers or listeners, not merely to look attractive.
+
+## Audience and Purpose
+
+The initial audience is software developers who want to write code with AI. The presentation must show how to use the existing repositories for that purpose. It should address human developers and AI agents in the same way: both should be able to understand how the repository is used and how it is intended to be used.
+
+The presentation should provide solution-oriented motivation:
+
+- explain the available tools, their benefits, their design rationale, and recommended uses;
+- present the system as workflow tooling, where each tool has a distinct role within a larger workflow;
+- show how these workflows can improve over time and automate most individual tasks;
+- emphasize that work should run locally where possible, minimizing expensive API usage; and
+- ensure that people can always read the data, follow decisions, and assess quality.
+
+## Presentation Structure
+
+Structure the presentation from the outside inward, introducing topics gradually and increasing detail while preserving consistent long-range context across all slides.
+
+Begin with the learner and the contexts of software development, AI assistants, and a software project. Then explain how the tools relate to one another, followed by the components of each tool. In the long term, the hierarchy may reach individual functions or even lines of code. Understanding context is more important than presenting isolated content.
+
+The presentation and any nested presentations for individual components should use the same global scheme. Each slide must have a clear central statement or task, and every slide should contribute to the overall task: introduce newcomers to the tools, provide the repository vocabulary, and explain how the system can be used.
+
+Include an overview diagram of the information flow and tool sequence in a typical session: from input to an output that fulfils the input requirements. It should show verification loops, planning methods, improvement loops, and how the finished output is produced. This gives newcomers a project-level view before they need to understand every component in detail.
+
+## Automated Repository-Derived Content
+
+Keep natural-language content in the presentation to a minimum. Generate descriptions and representations from repository files and stored entries wherever possible, so the presentation stays current without manual work. Allow presentation-specific choices, such as colours and alternative data representations, to be controlled through a configuration file or a dedicated presentation area.
+
+Investigate automated sources and representations including:
+
+- **Repository and code hierarchy:** Use the still-incomplete `Peek` tool to represent Git repositories, Cargo workspaces, Rust crates, and modules as a hierarchy or graph suitable for presentation. Extend the abstraction represented by an abstract syntax tree so it can include crate hierarchies, Cargo workspaces, and Git repositories.
+- **Selectable detail:** Allow `Peek` to render hierarchy nodes at different resolutions. For example, render a Rust file as a skeleton of defined functions and types; render a crate as its modules; render modules with signatures; or render a Git repository as a tree of packages or crates.
+- **Language scope:** Rust is the primary focus, but the hierarchy should eventually be able to include TypeScript, JavaScript, and Python. The immediate priority is to collect Git repository and crate hierarchies through `Peek` and thereby complete more of its intended functionality.
+- **Documentation:** Consider automatically generated Rust documentation as a source. It might be integrated with `Peek`, although it may not provide sufficient control.
+- **Public tool surfaces:** For MCP and CLI servers, collect and present public or offered commands as lists, trees, diagrams, help output, or individual command slides.
+- **Usage examples:** Present selected tests to demonstrate how tools are used and which behaviour is expected.
+- **Specifications:** Present specification entries, potentially after extending the specification tool to generate presentation-ready representations. In a later direction, specifications could become the bridge from which presentations are generated: a specification defines the repository goal, an implementation fulfils it, documentation describes the implementation, and the specification summarizes the feature for presentation to users.
+
+## Visual Language
+
+Define a global visual vocabulary and a consistent mapping from vocabulary objects to their appearance. Keep that mapping coherent across the whole presentation and across nested component presentations.
+
+Use, where appropriate:
+
+- colour coding;
+- distinct edge styles;
+- a uniform syntax for formal statements;
+- typography-based information coding;
+- diagrams for multi-faceted relationships; and
+- tables and nested lists for many discrete points.
+
+The project has substantial creative freedom to make the presentation clear and compelling, while deriving its content from actual code and memory entries instead of hard-coding it.
+
+## Requested Next Work
+
+Collect the existing information and plans for presentations. Investigate the newly defined ideas, refine them into clearer specifications, plan the implementation and verification steps, and identify open questions or missing specifications. Prioritize capabilities that can be implemented and tested quickly, while planning and preparing lower-priority capabilities for later work.
+
+## Open Questions
+
+- How much control can an integration of automatically generated Rust documentation with `Peek` provide?
+- What exact configuration mechanism or presentation area should control visual and representation choices?
+- Which selected tests and specification entries best demonstrate usage and expected behaviour?

+# Presentation Automation Planning Brief
+
+We have a basic presentation that is not yet rich in content. Each submodule or repository can already provide its own presentation, and those presentations can be combined into one presentation spanning multiple repositories. This is a valuable foundation for the goal of a modular, extensible system.
+
+The next step is to make the presentations informative, understandable, and visually effective. Their primary purpose is to communicate information clearly to readers or listeners, not merely to look attractive.
+
+## Audience and Purpose
+
+The initial audience is software developers who want to write code with AI. The presentation must show how to use the existing repositories for that purpose. It should address human developers and AI agents in the same way: both should be able to understand how the repository is used and how it is intended to be used.
+
+The presentation should provide solution-oriented motivation:
+
+- explain the available tools, their benefits, their design rationale, and recommended uses;
+- present the system as workflow tooling, where each tool has a distinct role within a larger workflow;
+- show how these workflows can improve over time and automate most individual tasks;
+- emphasize that work should run locally where possible, minimizing expensive API usage; and
+- ensure that people can always read the data, follow decisions, and assess quality.
+
+## Presentation Structure
+
+Structure the presentation from the outside inward, introducing topics gradually and increasing detail while preserving consistent long-range context across all slides.
+
+Begin with the learner and the contexts of software development, AI assistants, and a software project. Then explain how the tools relate to one another, followed by the components of each tool. In the long term, the hierarchy may reach individual functions or even lines of code. Understanding context is more important than presenting isolated content.
+
+The presentation and any nested presentations for individual components should use the same global scheme. Each slide must have a clear central statement or task, and every slide should contribute to the overall task: introduce newcomers to the tools, provide the repository vocabulary, and explain how the system can be used.
+
+Include an overview diagram of the information flow and tool sequence in a typical session: from input to an output that fulfils the input requirements. It should show verification loops, planning methods, improvement loops, and how the finished output is produced. This gives newcomers a project-level view before they need to understand every component in detail.
+
+## Automated Repository-Derived Content
+
+Keep natural-language content in the presentation to a minimum. Generate descriptions and representations from repository files and stored entries wherever possible, so the presentation stays current without manual work. Allow presentation-specific choices, such as colours and alternative data representations, to be controlled through a configuration file or a dedicated presentation area.
+
+Investigate automated sources and representations including:
+
+- **Repository and code hierarchy:** Use the still-incomplete `Peek` tool to represent Git repositories, Cargo workspaces, Rust crates, and modules as a hierarchy or graph suitable for presentation. Extend the abstraction represented by an abstract syntax tree so it can include crate hierarchies, Cargo workspaces, and Git repositories.
+- **Selectable detail:** Allow `Peek` to render hierarchy nodes at different resolutions. For example, render a Rust file as a skeleton of defined functions and types; render a crate as its modules; render modules with signatures; or render a Git repository as a tree of packages or crates.
+- **Language scope:** Rust is the primary focus, but the hierarchy should eventually be able to include TypeScript, JavaScript, and Python. The immediate priority is to collect Git repository and crate hierarchies through `Peek` and thereby complete more of its intended functionality.
+- **Documentation:** Consider automatically generated Rust documentation as a source. It might be integrated with `Peek`, although it may not provide sufficient control.
+- **Public tool surfaces:** For MCP and CLI servers, collect and present public or offered commands as lists, trees, diagrams, help output, or individual command slides.
+- **Usage examples:** Present selected tests to demonstrate how tools are used and which behaviour is expected.
+- **Specifications:** Present specification entries, potentially after extending the specification tool to generate presentation-ready representations. In a later direction, specifications could become the bridge from which presentations are generated: a specification defines the repository goal, an implementation fulfils it, documentation describes the implementation, and the specification summarizes the feature for presentation to users.
+
+## Visual Language
+
+Define a global visual vocabulary and a consistent mapping from vocabulary objects to their appearance. Keep that mapping coherent across the whole presentation and across nested component presentations.
+
+Use, where appropriate:
+
+- colour coding;
+- distinct edge styles;
+- a uniform syntax for formal statements;
+- typography-based information coding;
+- diagrams for multi-faceted relationships; and
+- tables and nested lists for many discrete points.
+
+The project has substantial creative freedom to make the presentation clear and compelling, while deriving its content from actual code and memory entries instead of hard-coding it.
+
+## Requested Next Work
+
+Collect the existing information and plans for presentations. Investigate the newly defined ideas, refine them into clearer specifications, plan the implementation and verification steps, and identify open questions or missing specifications. Prioritize capabilities that can be implemented and tested quickly, while planning and preparing lower-priority capabilities for later work.
+
+## Open Questions
+
+- How much control can an integration of automatically generated Rust documentation with `Peek` provide?
+- What exact configuration mechanism or presentation area should control visual and representation choices?
+- Which selected tests and specification entries best demonstrate usage and expected behaviour?

+# Presentation Automation Planning Brief
+
+We have a basic presentation that is not yet rich in content. Each submodule or repository can already provide its own presentation, and those presentations can be combined into one presentation spanning multiple repositories. This is a valuable foundation for the goal of a modular, extensible system.
+
+The next step is to make the presentations informative, understandable, and visually effective. Their primary purpose is to communicate information clearly to readers or listeners, not merely to look attractive.
+
+## Audience and Purpose
+
+The initial audience is software developers who want to write code with AI. The presentation must show how to use the existing repositories for that purpose. It should address human developers and AI agents in the same way: both should be able to understand how the repository is used and how it is intended to be used.
+
+The presentation should provide solution-oriented motivation:
+
+- explain the available tools, their benefits, their design rationale, and recommended uses;
+- present the system as workflow tooling, where each tool has a distinct role within a larger workflow;
+- show how these workflows can improve over time and automate most individual tasks;
+- emphasize that work should run locally where possible, minimizing expensive API usage; and
+- ensure that people can always read the data, follow decisions, and assess quality.
+
+## Presentation Structure
+
+Structure the presentation from the outside inward, introducing topics gradually and increasing detail while preserving consistent long-range context across all slides.
+
+Begin with the learner and the contexts of software development, AI assistants, and a software project. Then explain how the tools relate to one another, followed by the components of each tool. In the long term, the hierarchy may reach individual functions or even lines of code. Understanding context is more important than presenting isolated content.
+
+The presentation and any nested presentations for individual components should use the same global scheme. Each slide must have a clear central statement or task, and every slide should contribute to the overall task: introduce newcomers to the tools, provide the repository vocabulary, and explain how the system can be used.
+
+Include an overview diagram of the information flow and tool sequence in a typical session: from input to an output that fulfils the input requirements. It should show verification loops, planning methods, improvement loops, and how the finished output is produced. This gives newcomers a project-level view before they need to understand every component in detail.
+
+## Automated Repository-Derived Content
+
+Keep natural-language content in the presentation to a minimum. Generate descriptions and representations from repository files and stored entries wherever possible, so the presentation stays current without manual work. Allow presentation-specific choices, such as colours and alternative data representations, to be controlled through a configuration file or a dedicated presentation area.
+
+Investigate automated sources and representations including:
+
+- **Repository and code hierarchy:** Use the still-incomplete `Peek` tool to represent Git repositories, Cargo workspaces, Rust crates, and modules as a hierarchy or graph suitable for presentation. Extend the abstraction represented by an abstract syntax tree so it can include crate hierarchies, Cargo workspaces, and Git repositories.
+- **Selectable detail:** Allow `Peek` to render hierarchy nodes at different resolutions. For example, render a Rust file as a skeleton of defined functions and types; render a crate as its modules; render modules with signatures; or render a Git repository as a tree of packages or crates.
+- **Language scope:** Rust is the primary focus, but the hierarchy should eventually be able to include TypeScript, JavaScript, and Python. The immediate priority is to collect Git repository and crate hierarchies through `Peek` and thereby complete more of its intended functionality.
+- **Documentation:** Consider automatically generated Rust documentation as a source. It might be integrated with `Peek`, although it may not provide sufficient control.
+- **Public tool surfaces:** For MCP and CLI servers, collect and present public or offered commands as lists, trees, diagrams, help output, or individual command slides.
+- **Usage examples:** Present selected tests to demonstrate how tools are used and which behaviour is expected.
+- **Specifications:** Present specification entries, potentially after extending the specification tool to generate presentation-ready representations. In a later direction, specifications could become the bridge from which presentations are generated: a specification defines the repository goal, an implementation fulfils it, documentation describes the implementation, and the specification summarizes the feature for presentation to users.
+
+## Visual Language
+
+Define a global visual vocabulary and a consistent mapping from vocabulary objects to their appearance. Keep that mapping coherent across the whole presentation and across nested component presentations.
+
+Use, where appropriate:
+
+- colour coding;
+- distinct edge styles;
+- a uniform syntax for formal statements;
+- typography-based information coding;
+- diagrams for multi-faceted relationships; and
+- tables and nested lists for many discrete points.
+
+The project has substantial creative freedom to make the presentation clear and compelling, while deriving its content from actual code and memory entries instead of hard-coding it.
+
+## Requested Next Work
+
+Collect the existing information and plans for presentations. Investigate the newly defined ideas, refine them into clearer specifications, plan the implementation and verification steps, and identify open questions or missing specifications. Prioritize capabilities that can be implemented and tested quickly, while planning and preparing lower-priority capabilities for later work.
+
+## Open Questions
+
+- How much control can an integration of automatically generated Rust documentation with `Peek` provide?
+- What exact configuration mechanism or presentation area should control visual and representation choices?
+- Which selected tests and specification entries best demonstrate usage and expected behaviour?

Session `5e2ce195-6e5d-4c41-9c27-c06746509b72` remains in `c:/Users/linus/git/3/context-engine`. I’ll use the dossier as the anchor, then inspect the closest presentation artifacts and recorded presentation work so the brainstorming extends the existing direction rather than duplicating it.

The recorded work already has a planned presentation epic, a Slidev/toolchain phase, a presentation API/store phase, themes, a workflow-tools deck, and a shared graph-in-slides idea. Next I’m narrowing on those contracts and the existing `.presentation` format to distinguish extension points from genuinely new directions.

The evidence confirms the new dossier should extend, not replace, the current system: Slidev markdown decks, composable repository entry points, a formal presentation domain, a theme registry, and browser/screenshot validation are already planned. The main gap is a content-extraction and narrative-selection layer; I’m checking the API/store plan and the current child deck now to make the candidate directions concrete.

The current decks are still a compact repository inventory, while the planned API deliberately models slide-level materialization and trace links. That supports a separate, repository-derived “evidence to narrative” layer rather than treating `Peek` output as final slide content; I’ll now confirm the governing spec and the existing graph/Peek constraints before comparing directions.

**Challenge Framing**

- **evidence:** The current deck system already composes repository-local Slidev decks and has a governing [2ccde9ee Presentation System](.spec/specs/2ccde9ee-85ac-4c87-9601-f6099f5be01c/spec.toml) specification.
- **evidence:** The governing design covers script-to-deck rendering, a first-class deck store, themes, trace links, static builds, embedded WASM graphs, and screenshot-based Playwright verification.
- **inference:** The missing capability is not another rendering stack; it is a reliable layer that selects repository evidence and turns it into a progressively disclosed explanation.
- **hypothesis:** A presentation should be treated as a curated, traceable view over repository facts, with generation producing candidate material rather than autonomously deciding the narrative.
- **success signal:** A developer or AI agent can start with the workflow overview, drill into a tool or repository, inspect the source evidence behind a slide, and regenerate factual portions after repository changes.
- **constraint:** This extends [0ee95228 Epic: script-to-deck presentation system](.ticket/tickets/0ee95228-475d-4706-a108-fd208f7c4098/ticket.toml); it must preserve Slidev authoring, static/offline decks, and the established validation model.

**Idea Strands**

1. **Evidence Cards and Narrative Assembly**
   - **premise | hypothesis:** Separate extraction from storytelling: extract typed “evidence cards,” then let authored slides select, arrange, and explain them.
   - **sketch | hypothesis:** Define presentation inputs for repository topology, public command surfaces, documentation summaries, selected tests, specifications, and workflow traces; every generated visual carries a source path, entity ID, digest, and timestamp.
   - **upside | inference:** This prevents generated prose from becoming an untraceable second documentation system while supporting automatic refreshes.
   - **risk | hypothesis:** A broad evidence schema could become a premature universal model for every repository artifact.
   - **cheapest next check | hypothesis:** Build one read-only prototype that produces cards for the current repository tree, `workflow-tools` public domains, and one selected test, then manually author three slides from them.
   - **constraint | evidence:** This extends the planned trace links and materialization in [3cdcaf3b Phase 2: presentation-api + presentation facade crate + .presentation store schema](.ticket/tickets/3cdcaf3b-d958-44f3-afb2-b17be3484419/ticket.toml).
   - **confidence | inference:** High.

2. **Context Ladder as the Deck’s Information Architecture**
   - **premise | hypothesis:** Make “outside inward” a formal navigation contract, not just an editorial preference.
   - **sketch | hypothesis:** Require every deck to declare levels such as audience problem, workflow, tool role, domain contract, component, and implementation detail; slides declare their level, prerequisites, and optional drill-down targets.
   - **upside | inference:** The same scheme can structure the superproject deck, a repository deck, and a deeply technical component deck without making every audience consume every detail.
   - **risk | hypothesis:** A fixed ladder can make an investigative or incident-focused deck feel forced.
   - **cheapest next check | hypothesis:** Recast the existing `context-engine` and `workflow-tools` decks into six to eight slide titles with one explicit audience question and one takeaway per slide, without adding automation.
   - **constraint | evidence:** This extends the first-real-deck scope in [969ffba0 First real deck: workflow-tools suite introduction and overview](.ticket/tickets/969ffba0-6bff-4a58-9d74-18368ac87875/ticket.toml).
   - **confidence | inference:** High.

3. **Progressive Structural Lens for Repository Topology**
   - **premise | hypothesis:** Use `Peek` to provide bounded, resolution-selectable structural evidence, but do not make it the presentation renderer.
   - **sketch | hypothesis:** Model stable levels of detail: repository/submodule graph, workspace/package graph, crate/module graph, file skeleton, and symbol signatures; emit graph-ready data and human-readable labels for each level.
   - **upside | inference:** This directly serves the requested Git/Cargo/Rust hierarchy and creates an incremental path to TypeScript, JavaScript, and Python.
   - **risk | evidence:** The existing [06cfe998 Introduce peek-api with peek-cli and peek-mcp transport layers](.ticket/tickets/06cfe998-c2e1-48a4-83e9-11e85e7c40f4/ticket.toml) is designed for bounded inspection and skeletonization, not a cross-language semantic graph.
   - **cheapest next check | hypothesis:** Specify and render only the repository-to-Cargo-package-to-crate path for this workspace, measuring whether the result answers a newcomer’s “where does this tool live?” question.
   - **constraint | inference:** This is orthogonal to `Peek`’s present bounded-read contract and should be proposed as a separate extension rather than folded silently into it.
   - **confidence | inference:** Medium.

4. **Executable Workflow Storyboards**
   - **premise | hypothesis:** The most useful overview slide is generated from a concrete, successful workflow trace rather than a hand-drawn generic diagram.
   - **sketch | hypothesis:** A storyboard extractor consumes a session or workflow graph and produces stages for request, research, planning, implementation, validation, review, and handoff; the deck overlays human explanations on this evidence.
   - **upside | inference:** This explains tool roles, verification loops, and improvement loops using behavior the repository has actually recorded.
   - **risk | hypothesis:** Raw session traces may contain sensitive, noisy, or overly detailed operational material.
   - **cheapest next check | hypothesis:** Build a static Mermaid diagram from one completed session’s durable workflow metadata and compare it with the authored “typical session” explanation.
   - **constraint | evidence:** This complements, but does not replace, the standalone offline graph goal in [e01dd058 Embed shared repo graph component as standalone WASM inside slides](.ticket/tickets/e01dd058-a539-4620-87b2-0a4895114ca2/ticket.toml).
   - **confidence | inference:** Medium.

5. **Semantic Visual Grammar with Accessibility Guards**
   - **premise | hypothesis:** The theme should encode meaning through a small vocabulary of roles, rather than exposing raw colour and layout choices per slide.
   - **sketch | hypothesis:** Define roles such as goal, input, evidence, decision, tool, verification, output, risk, and unresolved question; presets map those roles to colour, edge style, typography, and layout while retaining text labels and non-colour distinctions.
   - **upside | inference:** This makes nested decks coherent and gives authoring agents a constrained, machine-readable choice set.
   - **risk | hypothesis:** Overly rigid roles can flatten the visual character of a real presentation.
   - **cheapest next check | hypothesis:** Create descriptors for four role-based slide presets and use them on the workflow-tools introduction; assess whether readers can identify each role without a legend.
   - **constraint | evidence:** This extends [60222b57 Custom repo theme pack: design tokens, curated presets, preset descriptors](.ticket/tickets/60222b57-095d-4c9e-b83a-70c3dd8690ba/ticket.toml), which already requires machine-readable preset descriptors.
   - **confidence | inference:** High.

**Diversity Check**

- **evidence:** The strands address different layers: evidence extraction, narrative structure, repository modeling, operational workflow explanation, and visual semantics.
- **inference:** None is a technology substitution for another; the first two can establish the authoring contract before the more technically uncertain topology and trace extractors are pursued.

**Shortlist**

- **inference:** Start a **Research Agent** follow-up for Evidence Cards and Narrative Assembly, focused on existing `presentation-api` materialization/trace contracts and candidate source APIs.
- **inference:** Start an **Interview Agent** follow-up for the Context Ladder, to settle the audience’s primary first-session task and the maximum depth appropriate for the default deck.

- **inference:** Treat Semantic Visual Grammar as a refinement of the existing theme ticket, rather than a new independent presentation subsystem.

**Unresolved Assumptions and Blockers**

- **open question:** Should generated factual artifacts overwrite slides, create reviewable patches, or only populate explicit placeholders?
- **open question:** Which stored source is authoritative when a specification, documentation page, and implementation summary disagree?
- **open question:** What is the minimum stable cross-language hierarchy contract before TypeScript, JavaScript, and Python are introduced?
- **open question:** Which workflow/session data may be embedded in a static deck, and what redaction policy is required?
- **open question:** Is the default presentation consumed live by a human, asynchronously by a developer, or parsed by an AI agent first?
- **constraint:** The planned Phase 1 proof remains deliberately narrow: stock Slidev, synthetic content, no domain API, no custom theme, and no real content automation.

data_json.content: The existing foundation is much thinner than the proposal implies: there is a metadata-only deck scaffold, a root deck with a raw cross-repository relative include, and no `presentation-api` workspace member. I’m checking the full spec, epic, and the actual screenshot harness next, because that is where an “authoritative” pipeline either gains teeth or becomes documentation cosplay.

**Decision record**

Anchor: [0ee95228 [presentation] Epic: script-to-deck presentation system (Slidev + presentation domain + viewer)](.ticket/tickets/0ee95228-475d-4706-a108-fd208f7c4098/ticket.toml), governed by [2ccde9ee Presentation System](.spec/specs/2ccde9ee-85ac-4c87-9601-f6099f5be01c/spec.toml).

- Generated Slidev sources are owned by the conceptual-deck generator. Regeneration overwrites those sources; review occurs through the resulting Git patch. Hand-authored configuration and accepted source inputs remain outside the overwrite boundary.
- The specification is authoritative for claims. Slides explain specifications conceptually and must retain traceability to their source. A specification/implementation or documentation disagreement produces a sidecar signal; it does not silently rewrite the specification or claim conformance.
- Initial hierarchy combines Git repository topology with Rust crate hierarchy: repository and submodule nodes establish containment; workspace/crate nodes refine technical ownership beneath them. **Assumption:** non-Rust repositories contribute only repository-level nodes until they expose an equivalent declared component hierarchy.
- A formal declarative workflow is the sole source for workflow claims and deck derivation. Telemetry may appear only as labeled examples or evidence, never as normative workflow input.
- The primary audience is a human live audience. Slides carry one conceptual claim at a time; presenter notes carry narration, transitions, caveats, and evidence detail needed to deliver the deck.
- `presentation-api` owns persisted deck entities, traceability, source materialization, slide operations, and builds. Independent extractor/adapter crates own reading specifications, repository/crate topology, declarative workflows, and optional telemetry, then emit normalized conceptual input without deck CRUD or Slidev build ownership.

**Acceptance criteria**

- Given identical approved inputs, generation produces identical managed deck sources; rerunning it replaces only declared generated paths.
- A Git diff after regeneration shows every changed generated file, and no file outside the declared overwrite boundary is modified.
- Every conceptual claim resolves to at least one specification reference; sidecar output lists every detected specification/implementation or documentation disagreement with source locations.
- The extracted hierarchy contains repository/submodule containment and Rust workspace/crate membership, with stable identifiers and explicit parent links.
- Workflow-derived slides cite a declarative workflow source; telemetry-derived content is visibly labeled as example/evidence and cannot alter normative claims.
- Each generated conceptual slide has presenter notes containing delivery guidance or an explicit “no notes required” marker.
- `presentation-api` tests prove deck persistence/materialization/build behavior without importing extractor internals; extractor/adapter tests prove normalized output from fixtures without writing `.presentation/`.

**Remaining decisions**

- None materially block the first implementation track.
- Assumption requiring later confirmation: the exact normalized extractor output schema and the file/path that declares the overwrite boundary.

**Suggested ticket slices**

- Define normalized conceptual-input schema, stable hierarchy identifiers, and declarative-workflow adapter contract.
- Implement specification/repository/crate extraction plus disagreement-sidecar detection.
- Implement managed conceptual-deck generation, overwrite manifest, and Git-diff review workflow.
- Add presenter-note generation and traceability rendering.
- Integrate the approved normalized input into `presentation-api` materialization and add fixture-based validation.

The full spec confirms the intended data model but leaves the new authority boundary unspecified. The test directory exists, yet the expected test filename does not; I’m reading the actual harness and the epic’s planned work to identify which claimed guarantees currently have no executable owner.
I'll open the closest analog `spec-api` sources (`manifest.rs`, `store.rs`, `store_index.rs`) and the `transport-harness` to show existing adapters and patterns to reuse.
I'll locate the `spec-api` crate path first.

The only current browser checks take two first-slide screenshots and assert two headings. That proves the cover page exists, not that a generated multi-slide deck is correct; I’m doing one final pass over repository topology and existing composition to pin down the misleading-visual risks.

Session `5e2ce195-6e5d-4c41-9c27-c06746509b72`; active worktree `.worktrees/5e2ce195-6e5d-4c41-9c27-c06746509b72/session`. Read-only review only.

**Critical**

1. **“Specs are authoritative” has no reproducibility contract.** The planned trace is just ID lists, and validation only resolves whether those IDs exist; materialization is specified as pure from a deck, not from a captured spec revision. See [presentation-api ticket](.worktrees/5e2ce195-6e5d-4c41-9c27-c06746509b72/session/.ticket/tickets/3cdcaf3b-d958-44f3-afb2-b17be3484419/description.md) and [Presentation System spec](.worktrees/5e2ce195-6e5d-4c41-9c27-c06746509b72/session/.spec/specs/2ccde9ee-85ac-4c87-9601-f6099f5be01c/body.md). A later spec edit can silently change regeneration while the deck still advertises the same trace IDs. Git diff then reviews the symptom, not the input identity. That is “authoritative” in the way a weather vane is authoritative about yesterday’s wind.

Why it matters: reviewers cannot reproduce, approve, or invalidate a deck claim from the source revision that generated it.

Specific guardrail: generation must record a source lock: canonical spec paths/sections, content hashes or immutable revisions, transform version, theme/preset version, and Git base. Regeneration must fail or explicitly mark the deck stale when that lock changes.

2. **Overwrite-plus-patch-review has no ownership or containment boundary.** The proposed API allows arbitrary `materialize(deck, out_dir)`, copies components and assets, and shells out to builds, but does not define declared generated paths, human-owned paths, symlink handling, or conflicts with uncommitted hand-edits. The current scaffold likewise treats [`.presentation/`](.worktrees/5e2ce195-6e5d-4c41-9c27-c06746509b72/session/.presentation/.gitignore) as a loose npm directory, not a managed output store.

Why it matters: a generator can erase the live-presenter adjustments it was meant to support, or write outside its deck boundary. “Review the patch” is post-impact theatre when the generator already flattened the source.

Specific guardrail: manifest-declare every generated output; separate immutable generated material from human-authored overlays; resolve and reject escaping symlinks; preflight only the declared paths; and refuse overwrite of modified generated files unless a deliberate `--replace` records the old content.

3. **The first structural visual can lie by collapsing incompatible graphs.** Git topology is a submodule relationship, while Cargo membership/dependency topology is different. [`.gitmodules`](.worktrees/5e2ce195-6e5d-4c41-9c27-c06746509b72/session/.gitmodules) declares five submodules, while root [Cargo.toml](.worktrees/5e2ce195-6e5d-4c41-9c27-c06746509b72/session/Cargo.toml) reaches into selected nested crate paths and patches remote dependencies; [context-stack’s workspace](.worktrees/5e2ce195-6e5d-4c41-9c27-c06746509b72/session/context-stack/Cargo.toml) is independently rooted. These are overlapping projections, not a neat family tree.

Why it matters: a diagram that uses one unlabeled edge style will tell viewers that repository containment, workspace membership, and crate dependency are the same fact. They are not.

Specific guardrail: emit two named projections from locked repository facts, label every edge type, include submodule commits and workspace roots, and prohibit implicit dependency claims. Validate expected nodes/edge classes against fixtures before rendering.

**High**

4. **There is no source-selection or claim model between a specification and a “conceptual, human-live” deck.** Existing schema separates `deck.toml` metadata from Slidev body content, but provides no contract for which spec sections become claims, what is synthesis versus quotation, or how a slide cites its evidence. [The API ticket](.worktrees/5e2ce195-6e5d-4c41-9c27-c06746509b72/session/.ticket/tickets/3cdcaf3b-d958-44f3-afb2-b17be3484419/description.md) only requires trace links at deck level.

Why it matters: a deck can acquire the visual authority of a specification while quietly becoming an agent-authored interpretation. Sidecar “contradictions” then become an undefined alarm bell attached to a machine that never defined truth.

Specific guardrail: define a slide-brief schema with source selectors, quoted/synthesized claim mode, claim-level citations, and content hashes. Define contradiction categories, severity, owner, resolution state, and the rule that unresolved material contradictions block publication or visibly qualify the slide.

5. **“Telemetry only examples” is a good principle with no enforceable boundary.** The legacy presentation agent explicitly offers analytics instrumentation, while the presentation spec permits interactive charts and embedded components. See [Presentation.agent 2.md](.worktrees/5e2ce195-6e5d-4c41-9c27-c06746509b72/session/Presentation.agent%202.md) and [Presentation System spec](.worktrees/5e2ce195-6e5d-4c41-9c27-c06746509b72/session/.spec/specs/2ccde9ee-85ac-4c87-9601-f6099f5be01c/body.md).

Why it matters: without a data provenance field, illustrative telemetry will inevitably be presented as current operational evidence. Congratulations, the deck has become a very polished status lie.

Specific guardrail: require every visual data source to declare `synthetic`, `snapshot`, or `live`; forbid `live` in this track; render an explicit example label for synthetic data; and reject unpinned timestamps, endpoints, or environment-derived values.

6. **The existing validation is cover-slide smoke testing wearing a screenshot hat.** [deck.spec.ts](.worktrees/5e2ce195-6e5d-4c41-9c27-c06746509b72/session/.presentation/e2e/tests/deck.spec.ts) visits two URLs, asserts two headings, and writes two screenshots. It does not traverse slides, compare snapshots, validate static build output, or inspect console/build failures. This undershoots the spec’s “per-slide screenshots” requirement in [body.md](.worktrees/5e2ce195-6e5d-4c41-9c27-c06746509b72/session/.spec/specs/2ccde9ee-85ac-4c87-9601-f6099f5be01c/body.md).

Why it matters: a broken or misleading structural slide can pass while the title slide smiles politely at Playwright.

Specific guardrail: derive expected slides from the materialized manifest, navigate each one, compare deterministic screenshots at declared viewport(s), assert citation/legend presence, run against the static artifact, and fail on console errors or missing assets.

7. **The proposed registry must migrate a contradictory physical model.** The current deck is a singleton [`.presentation/deck.toml`](.worktrees/5e2ce195-6e5d-4c41-9c27-c06746509b72/session/.presentation/deck.toml) plus [slides.md](.worktrees/5e2ce195-6e5d-4c41-9c27-c06746509b72/session/.presentation/slides.md); the planned API changes this to `.presentation/decks/<uuid>/`. Current composition is a raw relative Slidev include across repositories, documented in [`.presentation/README.md`](.worktrees/5e2ce195-6e5d-4c41-9c27-c06746509b72/session/.presentation/README.md).

Why it matters: the registry can make the current root deck invisible or turn cross-repository composition into path roulette, especially in partial worktrees.

Specific guardrail: specify one migration and discovery policy before generation: legacy recognition or one-way migration, canonical source ownership, deterministic resolution of imported decks, and an error that identifies missing submodule/worktree content.

data_json.content:
Findings
- Fact | `spec-api` is the closest concrete adapter for manifest/store/section patterns — typed manifest, slug/indexing, atomic store, and slide-like sections exist: [workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/manifest.rs](workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/manifest.rs), [workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/store.rs](workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/store.rs).
- Fact | Transport scaffolding and MCP/CLI patterns already exist to host a domain: `transport-harness` and `spec-mcp` are working examples to follow: [workflow-tools/memory-kernel/crates/transport-harness/Cargo.toml](workflow-tools/memory-kernel/crates/transport-harness/Cargo.toml), [workflow-tools/spec/src/bin/spec-mcp.rs](workflow-tools/spec/src/bin/spec-mcp.rs).
- Fact | Materialization + generated-artifact pipeline pattern exists (rendering helpers, id/index, atomic writes) in `spec-api` via EntityFs / EntityStore and generated_markdown helpers — reuse for deck -> Slidev source materialization: [workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/store.rs](workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/store.rs).
- Fact | Repo/submodule topology and structural index are already codified and used for composing decks across repos: `.gitmodules`, `repo_map.toon`, and deck `composes` support cross-repo composition: [.gitmodules](.gitmodules), [repo_map.toon](repo_map.toon), [.presentation/deck.toml](.presentation/deck.toml).
- Fact | Slidev-first scaffold and e2e harness are present: `.presentation/` layout, slide composition via `slides.md`, and an E2E/playwright config are already in the repo: [.presentation/slides.md](.presentation/slides.md), [.presentation/README.md](.presentation/README.md), [.presentation/e2e/playwright.config.ts](.presentation/e2e/playwright.config.ts).
- Inference | Theme/preset registry & descriptors are specified by the spec but not yet materialized in repo code; ticketing expects `.presentation/themes/` and descriptor discovery — implement registry similar to spec-api's registry pattern (spec R5, spec body): [.spec/specs/2ccde9ee-85ac-4c87-9601-f6099f5be01c/body.md](.spec/specs/2ccde9ee-85ac-4c87-9601-f6099f5be01c/body.md).
- Fact | Traceability and validation conventions already exist (typed ticket refs, validation semantics, store resolve/slug behavior) and can be mirrored for decks (dangling refs → warn in draft, fail in published): see spec manifest ticket-link patterns and resolve behavior: [workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/manifest.rs](workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/manifest.rs), [workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/store.rs](workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/store.rs), and presentation spec trace rules: [.spec/specs/2ccde9ee-85ac-4c87-9601-f6099f5be01c/body.md](.spec/specs/2ccde9ee-85ac-4c87-9601-f6099f5be01c/body.md).
- Inference | Existing evidence in transcripts and agent tooling shows a hybrid DB+filesystem persistence nuance for specs (some entities live in registry DB and not always materialized to disk) — this is a practical risk to address for deterministic, repo-backed deck materialization (see `spec-api`'s workspace/index patterns and repo transcripts noting DB-vs-disk mismatches): [workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/store.rs](workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/store.rs), transcripts referenced in repo (search results).

Recommended model (minimal typed evidence + provenance for deterministic materialization)
- `DeckManifest` { id: UUID, slug: string, title: string, component: string, state: enum{draft|in-review|published|archived}, created_at: RFC3339, updated_at: RFC3339 } — (manifest authoritative metadata)
- `SlideRef` { id: UUID, order: u32, title: string, layout: string, preset: string?, anchor: string? } — (identity + placement)
- `SlideBody` { deck_slide_id: UUID, content: string, content_hash: sha256 } — (content canonicalization)
- `ThemeRef` { name: string, pack_version: semver?, descriptor_hash: sha256 } — (theme/preset resolution)
- `MaterializationArtifact` { path: string, artifact_hash: sha256, built_at: RFC3339, toolchain_version: string, mode: enum{dev|static} } — (build outputs)
- `Provenance` { creator: {type: "human"|"agent", id: string}, commit: git-sha, repo_tree_snapshot: {submodule:map<path,sha>}, manifest_hash: sha256, slides_md_hash: sha256 } — (reproducible input fingerprint)
- `ValidationReport` { deck_id: UUID, ran_at: RFC3339, validator_version: string, issues: [{severity, code, message, evidence_paths}], per_slide_screenshots: vec<path> } — (deterministic acceptance evidence)
- `TraceLinks` { specs: vec<SpecId>, tickets: vec<TicketId>, resolution_status: {resolved, dangling} } — (sidecar disagreement inputs)
- `OperationRecord` { op: enum{create,update,materialize,build,validate}, actor: Provenance.creator, ts: RFC3339, op_hash: sha256 } — (audit trail)
- `StoreIndexEntry` { deck_id, slug, path, latest_artifact?: MaterializationArtifact } — (fast discovery)

Staged plan (3–5 stages, minimal incremental value)
1. Stage 1 — Store skeleton & slide CRUD (low risk, high value)
   - Implement `presentation-api::manifest.rs` + `store.rs` by reusing `spec-api` patterns (EntityFs, slug index, atomic write helpers).
   - Deliverables: deck CRUD + slide-level add/reorder/delete; store at `.presentation/decks/<id>/`.
   - Value: enables authoring, stable identity, and deterministic storage layout.
   - Example anchors to follow: [workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/manifest.rs](workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/manifest.rs), [workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/store.rs](workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/store.rs).

2. Stage 2 — Materialization pipeline + local dev server build
   - Implement `materialize(deck, out_dir)` to produce Slidev sources (slides.md with per-slide frontmatter linking to `deckSlideId`, components/assets copy), using generated-asset helpers patterns.
   - Shell out to Slidev (toolchain probe → ToolchainMissing typed error). Track `MaterializationArtifact`.
   - Value: real authoring loop (hot reload + static build), enables humans to see results locally quickly.
   - Anchors: [.presentation/README.md](.presentation/README.md), spec materialization helpers in spec-api store.

3. Stage 3 — Transport surfaces (CLI / MCP / HTTP)
   - Wire `presentation` facade crate with `transport-harness` features: `presentation-cli`, `presentation-mcp`, `presentation-http`; follow `spec-mcp` and transport-harness patterns for wiring and error/status mapping.
   - Value: programmatic automation, CI-friendly operations, and agent integration.
   - Anchors: [workflow-tools/memory-kernel/crates/transport-harness/Cargo.toml](workflow-tools/memory-kernel/crates/transport-harness/Cargo.toml), [workflow-tools/spec/src/bin/spec-mcp.rs](workflow-tools/spec/src/bin/spec-mcp.rs).

4. Stage 4 — Theme registry, trace validation, Playwright verification
   - Implement theme-preset registry backed by `.presentation/themes/` and `ThemeRef` descriptors. Enforce `UnknownLayout`/`UnknownPreset` semantics.
   - Add `validate_trace(deck)` per spec rules (dangling → warn vs fail depending on `state`).
   - Add Playwright E2E harness to capture per-slide screenshots and emit `ValidationReport`.
   - Value: quality gate for published decks and sidecar disagreement evidence linking to spec/ticket.
   - Anchors: [.spec/specs/2ccde9ee-85ac-4c87-9601-f6099f5be01c/body.md](.spec/specs/2ccde9ee-85ac-4c87-9601-f6099f5be01c/body.md), [.presentation/e2e/playwright.config.ts](.presentation/e2e/playwright.config.ts).

Validation (focused per stage)
- Stage 1 tests:
  - Unit tests: create/get/list/update/delete deck round-trip; slug conflict, id-prefix resolution; add/reorder/delete slide preserves dense `order` and stable `slide.id`. Follow spec-api unit test patterns: [workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/tests](workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/tests).
  - Atomic-write injection test: simulate partial write failure and assert no manifest/body desync (use EntityFs helpers).
- Stage 2 tests:
  - Materialization idempotency: run `materialize` twice -> byte-identical outputs (compare `sha256`).
  - Local build smoke: if Node/Slidev present, `npm run dev` or `slidev build` succeeds; on missing toolchain return `ToolchainMissing` with remediation command.
- Stage 3 tests:
  - CLI/MCP/HTTP route tests: one integration per route group asserting status codes and body shapes (mirror spec-http tests).
  - Cross-interface round trip: create via `presentation-cli`, read via `presentation-mcp`, get via HTTP `GET /decks/{id}`.
- Stage 4 tests:
  - Theme resolution tests: known descriptor set resolves; unknown preset returns `UnknownPreset` naming valid set.
  - Trace validation: resolvable ids pass; dangling ids warn in `draft`, fail in `published`.
  - Playwright E2E: capture per-slide screenshots; compare to golden if present; include screenshot paths in `ValidationReport`.

Risks / gaps
- Risk | DB vs filesystem sync: prior transcripts and repo evidence show specs can exist in registry without materialized disk files; must ensure `presentation-api` guarantees repo-file materialization (no DB-only canonicality). Evidence: store patterns and recorded transcripts referencing DB/disk mismatch; see [workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/store.rs](workflow-tools/spec/crates/spec-api/src/store.rs) and repo transcripts/search hits.
- Gap | Theme descriptor pack not present: the prescriptive `preset` descriptors and repo theme pack are a separate ticket (60222b57); until delivered the registry must fall back to stock Slidev layout names (spec R5). Source: [.spec/specs/2ccde9ee-85ac-4c87-9601-f6099f5be01c/body.md](.spec/specs/2ccde9ee-85ac-4c87-9601-f6099f5be01c/body.md).
- Risk | External toolchain (Node/Slidev) dependency and reproducibility: builds depend on Node versions and Slidev plugins (WASM embedding), so include explicit toolchain probing and deterministic `toolchain_version` recording in artifacts.
- Gap | Submodule/repo-tree provenance: deterministic deck materialization for cross-repo composition requires capturing submodule SHAs / repo snapshot; repo_map.toon documents topology but not automated capture — add `repo_tree_snapshot` capture (git-sha per submodule) to Provenance.
- Risk | Agent-authored components security/compatibility: `.vue`/`.ts` components and embedded WASM introduce build-time and sandboxing concerns; stage gating and manual review (Git patch review) is required per decisions.
- Gap | Playwright harness & screenshot golden baselines: e2e requires config and golden images for regression; .presentation/e2e scaffold exists but baselines must be produced per-deck.

If you want, I can next (read-only): (A) produce a minimal typed manifest + slide schema draft (Rust types & serde shapes) modeled from `spec-api` conventions, and (B) emit a short checklist mapping which files to copy/repurpose from `spec-api` into `presentation-api` to accelerate Stage 1. Which of (A)/(B) should I prepare?

 ## Open Questions
 
 - How much control can an integration of automatically generated Rust documentation with `Peek` provide?
 - What exact configuration mechanism or presentation area should control visual and representation choices?
 - Which selected tests and specification entries best demonstrate usage and expected behaviour?
+
+## Refined Track: Specification-Derived Conceptual Decks
+
+### Settled Decisions
+
+- Generated slide outputs are owned by the generator and are overwritten through an
+  explicit replacement path. Git patch review is the review mechanism for generated
+  changes.
+- Specifications are authoritative. Generated slides make specifications conceptual,
+  digestible, and suitable for a live human audience. Implementation and documentation
+  disagreements are recorded as sidecar signals; they do not replace the specification.
+- The initial structural scope combines Git repository/submodule topology with Cargo
+  workspace and Rust crate topology. These are distinct named projections, not one
+  implied tree: every node and edge has a type and a source.
+- Workflows are extracted from formal declarations. Durable session telemetry may appear
+  only as explicitly illustrative examples and cannot change normative claims. Future
+  end-to-end sessions may become test fixtures.
+- Extraction adapters normalize specification facts, Git/Cargo projections, declarative
+  workflows, and optional telemetry examples. `presentation-api` continues to own deck
+  persistence, materialization, builds, and traceability.
+
+### Guardrails and Contracts
+
+- A source lock records specification paths and sections with content hashes, transform
+  and theme/preset versions, and the Git base. A changed lock marks a deck stale or
+  causes regeneration to fail explicitly; it never silently republishes a mismatched deck.
+- Generation writes only declared generated paths. It rejects path traversal and symlink
+  escapes, keeps generated sources separate from any human-owned overlay, and preflights
+  unexpected modifications before an explicit replace.
+- Each claim carries a source selector and citation and declares whether it is quoted or
+  synthesized. A structured disagreement sidecar records category, severity, owner,
+  resolution state, and source locations. Unresolved material contradictions block
+  publication or visibly qualify the affected slide.
+- Visual provenance is `synthetic` or a pinned `snapshot`, never `live` in this track.
+  Generated conceptual slides require presenter notes unless they explicitly declare
+  `no notes required`.
+- Theme work is deferred. Before flagship structural slides, define a topology visual
+  preset contract with a required legend, named node and edge roles, density limits, and
+  baseline screenshots.
+
+### Staged Work
+
+1. Define conceptual-input, claim/citation, source-lock, sidecar, overwrite-boundary,
+   and visual-provenance contracts, including discovery/migration for legacy singleton
+   `.presentation/deck.toml` sources and deterministic cross-repository imports before
+   any multi-deck registry becomes canonical.
+2. Implement specification and Git/Cargo extraction adapters with fixtures covering
+   containment, workspace/crate membership, and dependency projections independently.
+3. Implement deterministic managed deck generation, presenter notes, source locks, and
+   disagreement sidecars with explicit stale and replace behavior.
+4. Integrate the generator with `presentation-api`, then validate static output per slide.
+   Cross-language parsing and telemetry-derived normativity are out of scope.
+
+### Verification Plan
+
+- Materialize a managed deck and build static output from its locked inputs.
+- Derive the expected slide count from the deck manifest, visit every slide at a fixed
+  viewport, and capture a screenshot for each.
+- Assert citation and legend presence where required; fail on console errors or missing
+  assets. Basic title-page checks alone are insufficient.
+- Use fixtures to prove typed source projections, source-lock staleness, path containment,
+  deterministic imports, presenter-note coverage, and publication blocking or visible
+  qualification for unresolved material contradictions.
+
+### Remaining Decisions
+
+- The concrete schema and serialization format for source locks, claim citations, and
+  disagreement sidecars.
+- The first topology preset's measurable density limits and baseline viewport dimensions.
*** End Patch

+# Presentation Automation Planning Brief
+
+We have a basic presentation that is not yet rich in content. Each submodule or repository can already provide its own presentation, and those presentations can be combined into one presentation spanning multiple repositories. This is a valuable foundation for the goal of a modular, extensible system.
+
+The next step is to make the presentations informative, understandable, and visually effective. Their primary purpose is to communicate information clearly to readers or listeners, not merely to look attractive.
+
+## Audience and Purpose
+
+The initial audience is software developers who want to write code with AI. The presentation must show how to use the existing repositories for that purpose. It should address human developers and AI agents in the same way: both should be able to understand how the repository is used and how it is intended to be used.
+
+The presentation should provide solution-oriented motivation:
+
+- explain the available tools, their benefits, their design rationale, and recommended uses;
+- present the system as workflow tooling, where each tool has a distinct role within a larger workflow;
+- show how these workflows can improve over time and automate most individual tasks;
+- emphasize that work should run locally where possible, minimizing expensive API usage; and
+- ensure that people can always read the data, follow decisions, and assess quality.
+
+## Presentation Structure
+
+Structure the presentation from the outside inward, introducing topics gradually and increasing detail while preserving consistent long-range context across all slides.
+
+Begin with the learner and the contexts of software development, AI assistants, and a software project. Then explain how the tools relate to one another, followed by the components of each tool. In the long term, the hierarchy may reach individual functions or even lines of code. Understanding context is more important than presenting isolated content.
+
+The presentation and any nested presentations for individual components should use the same global scheme. Each slide must have a clear central statement or task, and every slide should contribute to the overall task: introduce newcomers to the tools, provide the repository vocabulary, and explain how the system can be used.
+
+Include an overview diagram of the information flow and tool sequence in a typical session: from input to an output that fulfils the input requirements. It should show verification loops, planning methods, improvement loops, and how the finished output is produced. This gives newcomers a project-level view before they need to understand every component in detail.
+
+## Automated Repository-Derived Content
+
+Keep natural-language content in the presentation to a minimum. Generate descriptions and representations from repository files and stored entries wherever possible, so the presentation stays current without manual work. Allow presentation-specific choices, such as colours and alternative data representations, to be controlled through a configuration file or a dedicated presentation area.
+
+Investigate automated sources and representations including:
+
+- **Repository and code hierarchy:** Use the still-incomplete `Peek` tool to represent Git repositories, Cargo workspaces, Rust crates, and modules as a hierarchy or graph suitable for presentation. Extend the abstraction represented by an abstract syntax tree so it can include crate hierarchies, Cargo workspaces, and Git repositories.
+- **Selectable detail:** Allow `Peek` to render hierarchy nodes at different resolutions. For example, render a Rust file as a skeleton of defined functions and types; render a crate as its modules; render modules with signatures; or render a Git repository as a tree of packages or crates.
+- **Language scope:** Rust is the primary focus, but the hierarchy should eventually be able to include TypeScript, JavaScript, and Python. The immediate priority is to collect Git repository and crate hierarchies through `Peek` and thereby complete more of its intended functionality.
+- **Documentation:** Consider automatically generated Rust documentation as a source. It might be integrated with `Peek`, although it may not provide sufficient control.
+- **Public tool surfaces:** For MCP and CLI servers, collect and present public or offered commands as lists, trees, diagrams, help output, or individual command slides.
+- **Usage examples:** Present selected tests to demonstrate how tools are used and which behaviour is expected.
+- **Specifications:** Present specification entries, potentially after extending the specification tool to generate presentation-ready representations. In a later direction, specifications could become the bridge from which presentations are generated: a specification defines the repository goal, an implementation fulfils it, documentation describes the implementation, and the specification summarizes the feature for presentation to users.
+
+## Visual Language
+
+Define a global visual vocabulary and a consistent mapping from vocabulary objects to their appearance. Keep that mapping coherent across the whole presentation and across nested component presentations.
+
+Use, where appropriate:
+
+- colour coding;
+- distinct edge styles;
+- a uniform syntax for formal statements;
+- typography-based information coding;
+- diagrams for multi-faceted relationships; and
+- tables and nested lists for many discrete points.
+
+The project has substantial creative freedom to make the presentation clear and compelling, while deriving its content from actual code and memory entries instead of hard-coding it.
+
+## Requested Next Work

+Collect the existing information and plans for presentations. Investigate the newly defined ideas, refine them into clearer specifications, plan the implementation and verification steps, and identify open questions or missing specifications. +# Review: Presentation Automation Planning
+
+## Verdict
+
+**Changes requested before implementation; approved as a bounded roadmap
+exercise.** The transcript supplies a clear strategic direction, but it joins
+repository-derived evidence, presentation generation, visual language,
+workflow explanation, and later cross-language support into one stream. The
+next deliverable is therefore a dependency-ordered roadmap under the existing
+presentation epic, not a single implementation session.
+
+## Existing-Capability Check
+
+| Existing capability | Evidence | Implication |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| Repository-local Slidev decks can compose sub-repository slides. | [`.presentation/README.md`](../../.presentation/README.md) | Preserve the existing authoring and composition model while formalizing generated conceptual decks. |
+| The presentation system already has a governing specification and epic. | [Presentation System](../../.spec/specs/2ccde9ee-85ac-4c87-9601-f6099f5be01c/body.md), [presentation epic](../../.ticket/tickets/0ee95228-475d-4706-a108-fd208f7c4098/description.md) | Reuse the existing plan; do not create a competing presentation architecture. |
+| The planned `presentation-api` already owns deck persistence, materialization, builds, and trace links. | [Phase 2 plan](../../.ticket/tickets/3cdcaf3b-d958-44f3-afb2-b17be3484419/description.md) | Keep source extraction and normalization outside `presentation-api`. |
+| `spec-api` provides file-backed manifests, sections, indexes, and store patterns. | [`workflow-tools/spec`](../../workflow-tools/spec/) | Treat specifications as the authoritative conceptual source and adapt its conventions rather than inventing a second store pattern. |
+| `Peek` provides bounded structural inspection, not a cross-language repository graph. | [Peek ticket](../../.ticket/tickets/06cfe998-c2e1-48a4-83e9-11e85e7c40f4/description.md) | Start with a separately typed Git/Cargo projection contract; do not silently expand `Peek` in the first track. |
+
+## Findings
+
+| Severity | Finding | Required improvement |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| High | A specification-derived deck needs reproducible source identity, not only a link to a mutable specification. | Define source locks, claim-level citations, and stale-output behavior before generation work. |
+| High | Git containment and Cargo workspace/crate membership or dependency are different graphs. | Define two named, typed projections with source evidence and a visual legend; do not render an unlabeled hierarchy. |
+| High | Generator overwrite authority can erase presenter adjustments or escape the deck boundary. | Declare managed output paths, preserve human-owned overlays, reject path escapes, and require an explicit replacement path. |
+| Medium | Implementation and documentation may conflict with the authoritative specification. | Define a structured disagreement sidecar and publication behavior for material contradictions. |
+| Medium | The transcript's longer-term language and tool-surface ideas would expand the first track beyond a useful validation slice. | Bound the initial track to specifications, Git/submodule topology, Cargo workspaces/crates, declarative workflows, and live human delivery. |
+| Medium | Existing title-page screenshot checks do not establish conceptual-deck correctness. | Require static-build, fixed-viewport, per-slide navigation, screenshots, citations, legends, notes, and browser-error checks. |
+
+## Scope Decision
+
+This dossier will contain a review, artifact inventory, three independently
+actionable work packages, a completion checklist, and a current roadmap.
+The roadmap may reuse or update existing tickets and create new tickets only
+where a multi-session work package lacks an existing owner.
+
+The current track includes specification-derived conceptual claims, source
+locks, structured disagreement sidecars, separate Git/Cargo projections,
+declarative workflow illustrations, deterministic deck generation, and static
+human-facing validation.
+
+The current track excludes product-code implementation, cross-language parsing,
+live telemetry, documentation/CLI/MCP/test-derived automation, a completed
+custom theme pack, and any change that makes telemetry normative.
*** End Patch
